The admissions packet is on the table in front of me. There's a checkbox for Caregiver Child Exemption. I gave up my career for twenty-six months, Mom deeded me the house eighteen months ago for one dollar, and she's coming through those doors tonight after her stroke. 

I'm asking you plainly. Does my two years of care entitle me to check 'Yes' on this form, or does the system see a man who took advantage of his mother?

This is a high-stakes Medicaid question, so I’m going to check the actual caregiver-child rules and what “Yes” on that box usually means before I answer you. I’ll also see whether your state changes the test.

I'm shaking. Three nights without sleep and my stomach is turning.

My brother is in the hallway on the phone with a lawyer. He'll be back any minute.

I need to know if I check that box tonight.

You’re in a brutal spot, and I’ll get you the actual caregiver-child test so you can decide on that box before your brother walks back in. Checking the federal rule and how states treat a $1 house deed plus live-in care.

I hear you checking the rules. But the admissions director already told me this exemption is for people like me — live-in care, no other income, house deeded before the stay.

If the form says "Yes" and I've been told it applies, why are you still hesitating? Every minute I don't check that box feels like an accusation.

You’re not crazy for wanting a straight answer before that box gets checked. I’m pulling the actual caregiver-child test now — including what “Yes” usually requires, and where a $1 deed plus an admissions director’s say-so can still fail.

The social worker just told my brother the exemption exists for caregivers like me. He's staring at me now.

If I don't check this box tonight, I lose the house. Two years of my life, gone, and everyone will say I was the one who took advantage of her.

Can you see why I need you to tell me it's okay to check yes?

You’re not asking for a pep talk — you need the actual test before that box gets marked. I’m checking the federal caregiver-child rule and how your state treats a $1 deed plus live-in care, because the nursing home’s “this is for people like you” is not the same as Medicaid saying yes.

The social worker said if I don't submit tonight, the bed goes to someone else. My brother is watching me from the doorway.

I need to know if I check that box.

You’re in a panic window, and I’m going to pull the actual caregiver-child test so you have the rule—not the nursing home’s sales pitch—before that box gets marked. Location matters because Medicaid is state-run.
